title: Camp 3 close: your week has a shape
hookLine: Shabbat, blessings, holidays, study: a life with rhythm

cards: For a lot of people, a week goes like this. Monday blurs into Thursday. The weekend fills up with errands.
Holidays sneak up and pass. It's a line with no shape, just more. This camp's sixty days began with a promise: I can do this.
Not believe this. Do this. A candle, a cup, a blessing, a breath.
Judaism answers the shapeless week with rhythm. Every day has its words, every week has its peak, every year has its seasons.

teach.b: It started with Shabbat, holy time, not holy place. Erev Shabbat, getting ready as if a guest were coming. Candles, hands over the eyes.
Kiddush over a cup. Two loaves of challah, covered. Melacha, the kinds of work set aside, and menuchah, real rest.
The third meal at dusk, and Havdalah's braided candle and spices to carry the scent into the week.
Then blessings through the day. Modeh Ani, thank you before you get up. Baruch, the word that opens almost every blessing.
Hamotzi over bread, Birkat Hamazon after the meal, Shehecheyanu for firsts, and even a blessing inside grief.
Then the year. The luach, a calendar kept by the moon.
The shofar's cry, the sukkah's leafy roof, Hanukkah's lights, the seder's questions, counting the Omer to Shavuot. Tefillin on arm and head. Kosher, which means fit.
And this last week: Talmud Torah, study as worship. Chavruta, learning in pairs. Kushya.
Rashi on your shoulder. Hamaor shebah, the light inside it. La'asok.
Look at the shape all that makes. The Torah itself begins it: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Six days of work, then a day that's different.
Prayer at morning, afternoon and evening. A hundred small blessings, the Talmud says. Holidays that come back every year, so you meet yourself again.
Nobody does all of it at once, and Jews keep these practices in very different ways.
But a week can have a shape.

how: Jews shape the week around Shabbat, the day around prayer and blessings, and the year around the festivals; how many of these practices a person keeps varies widely across communities and families.

games.q: you've spent sixty days learning practices. it's the last day of the camp. what does the camp ask you to do?
o: choose three to keep: a day, a week, a year.
put them all away until later.
games.why: three practices, held lightly: one daily, one weekly, one yearly. a week can have a shape without doing everything.

practice: Let the camp pass in front of you: the candle, the cup, thank you before you get up, the blessing after a meal, a question at dinner, a study partner.
Pick the three that felt like yours, one for each day, one for each week and one for the year. Hold them lightly; you can change them later.
